messages.subject: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Hi there,

I'm trying to specify custom initial values for an analysis I'm running. Right now, I go through the following steps:

  1. Estimate model with blavaan default initial values, I think inits = "prior" (using target = "jags")
  2. Extract initial values: myinits <- blavInspect(fit, "inits")
  3. Replace the values in "myinits" with my own initial values. For me, those values are housed in a named list: myinits$c1$parvec (one for each chain, c1, c2, c3, etc.).
  4. Estimate the model again using following code: bsem(model, data, inits = myinits, target = "jags").
This last step returns the following error:
Error : The list specified as the argument for inits (chain 1) was not a fully named list

Does anyone know what this means? I also tried to export the jags files (using mcmcfile = TRUE), reading in the .rda file, and extracting the inits from there, but that doesn't work either.

Do I need to name each element of the $parvec vector?

Thanks for any help/info!
Sonja

messages.subject: Re: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Sonja

I would recommend you to do this in a different way

1. Fit the model with lavaan
2. extract the parameterestimates table
3. change the values of the "est" column to what starting values you want to use
4. give the  new parameterestimates table to the inits argument, it will use the "est" column for initial values

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Hi Sonja,

I think Mauricio's strategy could work, but would restrict you to using the same initial values for each chain. But I also think your strategy is really close... I think the error means that some entry of myinits$c1 does not have a name. You could look at the names using

names(myinits$c1)

where the error suggests some names are "".

And then myinits$c1$parvec should just be a numeric vector, without any names. A second entry in c1, "ibpsi", also is used for models with unrestricted covariance matrices.

There is always the chance of a bug, and I can look at it some more if you can send code that leads to the error.

Best,
Ed

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Hi Sonja,

Thanks for the examples! I think there might indeed be a problem with sending in initial values using the model summary or parameter table. Those options are from the early days when you had to use jags (as opposed to the possibility of stan), and the options could use more of my recent attention.

I think the most reliable way to specify initial values is using a strategy related to the code below. But you have an extra complication because you are specifying an initial value for a covariance. blavaan internally breaks that covariance into variances and a correlation, so that the initial value is being specified for the correlation underneath the covariance. AND, due to the way that distributions are defined in jags, this correlation needs to be specified on a (0,1) scale instead of a (-1,1) scale. So, for example, if you wanted to specify a correlation of -.1, then the initial value is (1 + -.1)/2 = .45. In general, the covariances and covariance matrices are trickiest to deal with.

Ed

fit <- bcfa(mod_simple_cfa_0, data = dat_cfas, target='jags', n.chains=2, do.fit=FALSE,
            seed = c(2406, 1979))
myinits <- blavInspect(fit, 'inits')

## figuring out what is what:
myinits$c1
cbind(names(blavInspect(fit, 'jagnames')), myinits$c1$parvec)

## 16:18 are correlations underlying the covariances, but they are also
## scaled to be between 0 and 1 (technical issues related to beta distribution).
## So .9 on (-1,1) scale becomes (1 + .9)/2 = .95 on (0,1) scale. This is
## extreme and causes jags to crash. But I think
## you want the covariance to be .9, not the correlation, and I guess the
## correlation is much smaller (I haven't solved for it)
for (i in 1:2){
  myinits[[i]]$parvec[16:18] <- .95
}

## seed is already specified in the initial values, so no need for it again. If seed is
## specified again, I see the "not a fully named list" error.
fit <- bcfa(mod_simple_cfa_0, data = dat_cfas, target='jags', n.chains=2, inits = myinits)

messages.subject: Re: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Thank you, Ed! This is super helpful and clarifying, esp. the part about using a formula to specify initial values for the covariance/correlation :)

In my model, I fix the variances of the latent factors to 1 (so I can estimate all loadings). I always assumed that that meant that the covariance between the factors turns into a correlation (since it's standardized?). My issue with the default initial values is that it keeps pulling the covariance/correlation estimates towards .5, even if I run 400,000 iterations (200,000 burnin). 

But if I set the initial values to .9 or .95, then I get a runjags error: Error in node eta[1,3] Invalid parent values which I think means that the precision value in the ~dnorm() for eta[1,3] takes on an impossible initial value (negative maybe?). I tried an initial value of .7, but that just results in estimates close to .5, as the default initial values do.

I ran the analysis again with the first item loading fixed at 1 for each factor, and asked for standardized estimates, hoping that this might solve the issue since it switches the prior to the Wishart distribution. But the standardized estimates for the correlations are still way lower than .9 and they look very different compared to the same analysis run in lavaan with ML.

In addition, these issues don't arise for models with lower covariances/correlations. I'm not super familiar with the behavior of the beta prior (beta(1,1) is uniform on (0,1) and then you do some magic to apply it to (-1,1), right?), but is this prior known to push the posterior towards more moderate values?

Also, let me know if this is all too particular/not relevant and I should "close" this thread. You definitely helped me figure out the initial values issue, so at least I'm one step closer!

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Setting custom initial values?
parts:
Hi Sonja,

A few thoughts that may or may not help:

- Based on your description of the issues, I would guess the issue is more related to the prior than the initial values.

- You are right that the uniform beta is used by default on a correlation (and yes, it ends up being on (-1,1)). But there is also an unstated constraint that the combination of all correlations in the matrix has to lead to a positive definite matrix. This means that the uniform ends up being somewhat informative and pushes correlations closer to 0. The post below describes the issue well:

http://srmart.in/is-the-lkj1-prior-uniform-yes/

In practice, I think this means that the prior will tend to push correlations towards 0 unless you have lots of data. (You could check that by generating a huge dataset and seeing what changes.)

- It would be worth trying the model with target="stan" if you can, to make sure that you observe similar behavior there.

Ed

parts:
Hi Ed,

Apologies for taking a bit to get back to you, I had a busy week. 

I estimated the model with a simulated sample of 5,000 using target = "jags" and it still struggled with the high correlation: large Rhat values (> 10) even with many iterations, estimates of around .3. So, increasing the sample size to 5,000 does not appear to help much. I didn't go much bigger because my laptop started struggling and I don't currently have easy access to a more powerful computer.

I tried with target = "stan" and the estimates look much better (although it takes much longer to estimate with the same number of iterations), so it seems to be an issue of target = "jags" more than an issue with the beta prior itself. This is great news in general as most people already use blavaan with stan, but not really for my plan haha.

I was hoping to use target = "jags" for this specific project because I need to compare some estimates to output from Mplus and so I'd like to have both based on the Gibbs sampler (which I don't think is possible with stan since it uses HMC or NUTS...). Perhaps I just have to let it go for this project and see how similar the estimates are for the same dataset analyzed using target = "stan" and in Mplus.

Thanks for helping me think through this! I hope my explorations have been useful to you too in some way.

Sonja

Then blavaan does some things in the background to aid in convergence (which are triggered by std.lv=TRUE). So I would specify the model like this:

mod_simple_cfa_0 <- '
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
f2 =~ y6 + y7 + y8 + y9 + y10
f3 =~ y11 + y12 + y13 + y14 + y15 '

The factor correlations still have problems there, I guess because they are so large and because the blavaan parameterization is not great for this. In practice, you might also argue that this should be a one-factor model instead of three-factor model (but I realize you are probably using this model for a reason).

I tried with target = "stan" and the estimates look much better (although it takes much longer to estimate with the same number of iterations), so it seems to be an issue of target = "jags" more than an issue with the beta prior itself. This is great news in general as most people already use blavaan with stan, but not really for my plan haha.

One thing there is that the Stan samples are usually less autocorrelated, so you can usually get by with many fewer iterations as compared to JAGS. I typically compare them by "effective sample size per second", which takes into account autocorrelation and sampling time. There are some figures in the paper below that show what I am talking about:

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07733

I was hoping to use target = "jags" for this specific project because I need to compare some estimates to output from Mplus and so I'd like to have both based on the Gibbs sampler (which I don't think is possible with stan since it uses HMC or NUTS...). Perhaps I just have to let it go for this project and see how similar the estimates are for the same dataset analyzed using target = "stan" and in Mplus.

It might be possible to export the jags syntax and use different priors (say, a prior directly on the lv correlation matrix instead of the parameter expanded approach). But this would not be a trivial change.

Best,

Hi Sonja,

A few thoughts that may or may not help:

- Based on your description of the issues, I would guess the issue is more related to the prior than the initial values.

- You are right that the uniform beta is used by default on a correlation (and yes, it ends up being on (-1,1)). But there is also an unstated constraint that the combination of all correlations in the matrix has to lead to a positive definite matrix. This means that the uniform ends up being somewhat informative and pushes correlations closer to 0. The post below describes the issue well:

http://srmart.in/is-the-lkj1-prior-uniform-yes/

In practice, I think this means that the prior will tend to push correlations towards 0 unless you have lots of data. (You could check that by generating a huge dataset and seeing what changes.)

- It would be worth trying the model with target="stan" if you can, to make sure that you observe similar behavior there.

Ed

Thanks for the examples! I think there might indeed be a problem with sending in initial values using the model summary or parameter table. Those options are from the early days when you had to use jags (as opposed to the possibility of stan), and the options could use more of my recent attention.

I think the most reliable way to specify initial values is using a strategy related to the code below. But you have an extra complication because you are specifying an initial value for a covariance. blavaan internally breaks that covariance into variances and a correlation, so that the initial value is being specified for the correlation underneath the covariance. AND, due to the way that distributions are defined in jags, this correlation needs to be specified on a (0,1) scale instead of a (-1,1) scale. So, for example, if you wanted to specify a correlation of -.1, then the initial value is (1 + -.1)/2 = .45. In general, the covariances and covariance matrices are trickiest to deal with.

Ed

            seed = c(2406, 1979))

myinits$c1
cbind(names(blavInspect(fit, 'jagnames')), myinits$c1$parvec)

Sonja

Not specifc about the model, but the isea of comparing the results with Mplus. You can compare the model with Mplus, if the model is properly specify the posterior distributions should arrive to "about" the same result even with different samplers. The main differences of using Gibbs vs NUTS comes to be with higher order models, effective sample per econd measures, autocorrelations, and metrics like this.
If you are using the default priors in both, you might get different results based on this as the priors in Mplus are a lot wider than in blavaan.

Also, Mplus does not do the same Gibbs that JAGS do, they have made modifications on how they run, Mplus changes are to make it run faster.

Unless you you are looking for something very specific, I would say you can compare Mplus with blavaan target="stan"

## So .9 on (-1,1) scale becomes (1 + .9)/2 = .95 on (0,1) scale. This is
## extreme and causes jags to crash. But I think
## you want the covariance to be .9, not the correlation, and I guess the
## correlation is much smaller (I haven't solved for it)
for (i in 1:2){
  myinits[[i]]$parvec[16:18] <- .95
}

## seed is already specified in the initial values, so no need for it again. If seed is
## specified again, I see the "not a fully named list" error.
fit <- bcfa(mod_simple_cfa_0, data = dat_cfas, target='jags', n.chains=2, inits = myinits)

I estimated the model with a simulated sample of 5,000 using target = "jags" and it still struggled with the high correlation: large Rhat values (> 10) even with many iterations, estimates of around .3. So, increasing the sample size to 5,000 does not appear to help much. I didn't go much bigger because my laptop started struggling and I don't currently have easy access to a more powerful computer.

I looked at that code again and noticed one thing that helps a bit (but not completely). If you are fixing the factor variances to 1, you should use std.lv=TRUE in blavaan. Then blavaan does some things in the background to aid in convergence (which are triggered by std.lv=TRUE). So I would specify the model like this:

mod_simple_cfa_0 <- '
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
f2 =~ y6 + y7 + y8 + y9 + y10
f3 =~ y11 + y12 + y13 + y14 + y15 '

fit <- bcfa(mod_simple_cfa_0, data = dat_cfas, target='jags', n.chains=2, dp=dpriors(itheta="dgamma(1,.5)", ipsi="dgamma(1,.5)", target='jags'), burnin=1000, sample=500, std.lv=TRUE)

The factor correlations still have problems there, I guess because they are so large and because the blavaan parameterization is not great for this. In practice, you might also argue that this should be a one-factor model instead of three-factor model (but I realize you are probably using this model for a reason).


I tried with target = "stan" and the estimates look much better (although it takes much longer to estimate with the same number of iterations), so it seems to be an issue of target = "jags" more than an issue with the beta prior itself. This is great news in general as most people already use blavaan with stan, but not really for my plan haha.

One thing there is that the Stan samples are usually less autocorrelated, so you can usually get by with many fewer iterations as compared to JAGS. I typically compare them by "effective sample size per second", which takes into account autocorrelation and sampling time. There are some figures in the paper below that show what I am talking about:

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07733


I was hoping to use target = "jags" for this specific project because I need to compare some estimates to output from Mplus and so I'd like to have both based on the Gibbs sampler (which I don't think is possible with stan since it uses HMC or NUTS...). Perhaps I just have to let it go for this project and see how similar the estimates are for the same dataset analyzed using target = "stan" and in Mplus.

It might be possible to export the jags syntax and use different priors (say, a prior directly on the lv correlation matrix instead of the parameter expanded approach). But this would not be a trivial change.

Best,
Ed



On Friday, October 2, 2020 at 2:43:21 PM UTC-7 Ed Merkle wrote:
Hi Sonja,

A few thoughts that may or may not help:

- Based on your description of the issues, I would guess the issue is more related to the prior than the initial values.

- You are right that the uniform beta is used by default on a correlation (and yes, it ends up being on (-1,1)). But there is also an unstated constraint that the combination of all correlations in the matrix has to lead to a positive definite matrix. This means that the uniform ends up being somewhat informative and pushes correlations closer to 0. The post below describes the issue well:

http://srmart.in/is-the-lkj1-prior-uniform-yes/

In practice, I think this means that the prior will tend to push correlations towards 0 unless you have lots of data. (You could check that by generating a huge dataset and seeing what changes.)

- It would be worth trying the model with target="stan" if you can, to make sure that you observe similar behavior there.

Ed

Hi Sonja,

Thanks for the examples! I think there might indeed be a problem with sending in initial values using the model summary or parameter table. Those options are from the early days when you had to use jags (as opposed to the possibility of stan), and the options could use more of my recent attention.

I think the most reliable way to specify initial values is using a strategy related to the code below. But you have an extra complication because you are specifying an initial value for a covariance. blavaan internally breaks that covariance into variances and a correlation, so that the initial value is being specified for the correlation underneath the covariance. AND, due to the way that distributions are defined in jags, this correlation needs to be specified on a (0,1) scale instead of a (-1,1) scale. So, for example, if you wanted to specify a correlation of -.1, then the initial value is (1 + -.1)/2 = .45. In general, the covariances and covariance matrices are trickiest to deal with.

Ed

fit <- bcfa(mod_simple_cfa_0, data = dat_cfas, target='jags', n.chains=2, do.fit=FALSE,
            seed = c(2406, 1979))

myinits <- blavInspect(fit, 'inits')

## figuring out what is what:
myinits$c1
cbind(names(blavInspect(fit, 'jagnames')), myinits$c1$parvec)

## correlation is much smaller (I haven't solved for it)

  myinits[[i]]$parvec[16:18] <- .95
}
